reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Extremely rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by TF variants leading to absent or markedly reduced circulating transferrin
Paradoxical picture of severe iron-deficiency (microcytic hypochromic) anaemia together with progressive tissue iron overload
Without transferrin, iron cannot be delivered efficiently to erythroid precursors, so erythropoiesis is iron-starved despite abundant body iron
Unbound and non-transferrin-bound iron is deposited in liver, heart and other organs, causing haemosiderosis with hepatic and cardiac damage
Growth retardation and recurrent infections may accompany the anaemia in childhood
Diagnosis rests on very low or absent serum transferrin with high serum ferritin and tissue iron loading, confirmed by TF genetic testing
Management combines transferrin or plasma infusion to support erythropoiesis with measures to control iron overload such as iron chelation, avoiding inappropriate iron supplementation
reference.pathophysiology: Transferrin is the plasma glycoprotein that binds iron and delivers it to cells, especially erythroid precursors, via the transferrin receptor. In congenital atransferrinaemia the near-absence of transferrin means dietary and recycled iron cannot be transported to the bone marrow, so haemoglobin synthesis is impaired and a microcytic anaemia develops even though total body iron is high. The excess iron, unable to be handled by the normal transferrin pathway, is absorbed avidly from the gut and deposited as haemosiderin in parenchymal organs, producing progressive hepatic, cardiac and endocrine iron toxicity that resembles other iron-overload states.
additionalDifferentials: Hereditary haemochromatosis and secondary iron overload
Thalassaemia and other congenital anaemias with iron loading
additionalInvestigations: Serum transferrin and transferrin saturation (very low or absent transferrin)
Serum iron, total iron-binding capacity and ferritin (high ferritin with tissue loading)
Full blood count and film showing microcytic hypochromic anaemia
TF molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
Liver and cardiac iron assessment (e.g. MRI-based quantification) and organ function tests
Bone marrow evaluation where the anaemia is otherwise unexplained
redFlags: Cardiac dysfunction or arrhythmia from myocardial iron overload
Progressive hepatic dysfunction or fibrosis from iron deposition
Severe anaemia unresponsive to iron supplementation
Growth failure with recurrent serious infections in childhood
reference.prognosis: Early recognition with transferrin or plasma replacement to support haematopoiesis and control of iron overload can markedly improve outcome; untreated disease progresses to organ damage from iron deposition, particularly cardiac and hepatic, which determines long-term prognosis.
pitfalls: Treating the microcytic anaemia with iron supplementation, which worsens iron overload
Not recognising the paradox of anaemia with high ferritin and tissue iron
Confusing the picture with iron-refractory iron-deficiency anaemia or haemochromatosis
Overlooking early cardiac or hepatic iron loading before organ damage is advanced
references: Scriver's OMMBID (Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease)
management: Deliver transferrin through infusions of apotransferrin or fresh frozen plasma to support iron delivery to erythroid precursors and correct the microcytic anaemia
Treat the tissue iron overload with iron chelation therapy while strictly avoiding iron supplementation
Monitor with full blood count, ferritin and quantification of cardiac and hepatic iron loading by MRI-based techniques, alongside organ function tests
Manage the complications of parenchymal iron deposition affecting the heart, liver and endocrine organs
Prevent and treat the recurrent infections and support growth in childhood
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across haematology, cardiology, hepatology and endocrinology, and offer genetic counselling with family screening for this autosomal recessive disorder
